title: Netflix Bridges AWS IAM and Internal Identity with Workload Attestation
gist: Netflix built a workload attestation scheme that lets Apache Spark jobs on Amazon EMR trade their AWS IAM execution identity for a short-lived internal Metatron PKI certificate, with the driver attesting once on behalf of thousands of executors and Data Projects mapped to IAM roles spread across a pool of AWS accounts.

insights.claim: Netflix runs two identity systems: AWS IAM execution roles for managed workloads and Metatron, a private PKI issuing short-lived X.509 certificates for mutual TLS, so a Spark job on EMR must prove its AWS identity maps to its internal Data Project identity.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Multi-cloud and managed-compute identity federation is a recurring enterprise security cost.

insights.claim: The approach of exchanging an AWS identity for an internal one avoids manually injecting credentials into managed compute workloads.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.locator: The approach bridges AWS IAM with Netflix’s internal Metatron PKI

insights.claim: On managed infrastructure you cannot bootstrap identity freely as you can on self-built infrastructure, which motivated retaining the provider's identity as cryptographic proof.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Managed services constrain identity design; attestation patterns fill the gap.
insights.quote: On infrastructure you build yourself, you can bootstrap your own identity however you like.
insights.locator: Dhruv Pratap, Big Data Platform Engineer at Netflix

insights.claim: Each Data Project maps to a dedicated IAM role, and because Data Projects are expected to reach the tens of thousands, roles are deterministically distributed across a pool of dedicated AWS accounts.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Shows account-sharding as a scaling workaround for per-account IAM limits.
insights.locator: The design maps each Data Project to a dedicated IAM role

insights.claim: Netflix's control plane, the only service authorized to create workload claims, issues signed metadata, and the Spark driver submits a pre-signed AWS STS GetCallerIdentity request that the Identity service verifies with AWS before issuing a Metatron certificate from the intersection of both proofs.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Two-party proof (AWS role plus signed intent) prevents spoofing of workload identity.
insights.locator: When a job is submitted, Netflix’s control plane validates the request

insights.claim: Netflix has the Spark driver attest once and distribute credentials to executors over authenticated, encrypted Spark RPC, avoiding attestation traffic proportional to executor count but making the driver an additional trust boundary.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Trade-off between attestation load and a concentrated trust boundary.
insights.locator: The architecture also addresses Spark’s executor fan-out

insights.claim: The driver periodically re-attests before its short-lived certificate expires while executors do not renew independently, which Netflix says makes repeatable attestation important for long-running workloads.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Renewal design determines resilience for long jobs.
insights.locator: Credential renewal is handled separately from initial bootstrap

insights.claim: Netflix says the pattern, separating organizational workload identity from the managed compute provider while keeping the provider identity as proof, can apply to other managed environments where workloads get a cloud identity but need a separate organizational one.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A reusable pattern for multi-environment zero-trust adoption.
insights.locator: The pattern separates internal workload identity
